prompt: A stack backed by a dynamic array doubles capacity when a push finds it full, and **halves** capacity whenever a pop leaves length at half of capacity or less. It holds exactly 1,024 elements at capacity 1,024. A workload now alternates `push, pop, push, pop, ...` forever. What happens?

options.text: Each push doubles to 2,048 and each pop halves back to 1,024, so every operation copies about 1,000 elements
options.explanation: Correct. This is resize thrashing. The push at 1,024/1,024 grows to 2,048 (copying 1,024); the pop leaves 1,024/2,048, exactly half, so it shrinks back (copying 1,024). Every operation pays O(n). Shrinking only at one-quarter full prevents it.
The amortised guarantee breaks here: the policy lets a single cheap operation undo the resize just paid for.
The pops balance the pushes, so length oscillates around 1,024; capacity bounces rather than grows.

options.text: Nothing; the shrink never triggers because length never falls below 1,024
options.explanation: The rule fires at half *or less*, and after the push grows capacity to 2,048, a pop back to 1,024 is exactly half.

workedExample:
Trace from length 1,024, capacity 1,024:

```
op    len   cap   resize
push  1025  2048  grow, copy 1024
pop   1024  1024  shrink, copy 1024
push  1025  2048  grow, copy 1024
pop   1024  1024  shrink, copy 1024
```

Every single operation copies about 1,000 elements, so the 'amortised O(1)' stack is now O(n) per operation, where n is the number of elements (about 1,024).

Fix: **shrink to half only when length falls to a quarter of capacity**. After growing to 2,048, you'd need to pop down to 512 before shrinking, so at least about n/2 cheap operations separate any two resizes. That restores amortised O(1). (Even a strict 'below half' rule is fragile: a push, pop, pop, push, push pattern still thrashes.)
